say: Why would a truck maker raise its offer by thirty cents? On the ninth of October, Tata Motors lifted its offer for Iveco Group from fourteen euros ten to fourteen euros forty a share.
Its slide gives the company's reason: 'the slight delay in the completion of the Offer'. The most the offer could now cost: about forty two thousand, five hundred and sixty one crore rupees.
Now the other half. The same results show forty two percent more vehicles wholesaled than a year earlier. Revenue, up forty two percent too. Yet less operating profit from each rupee of sales.
So our question: what did this quarter show about the truck business, and what do the filings say about the Iveco offer's cost?

First, which Tata Motors? Last year the company split in two. The commercial vehicle business went to TML Commercial Vehicles, now named Tata Motors Limited. The old Tata Motors, now Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles, kept the passenger vehicles.

So where did forty two percent come from? One hundred and thirty five thousand vehicles in three months. Every segment grew by double digits. Heavy trucks rose forty one percent, small commercial vehicles and pickups twenty seven, passenger carriers thirty one, and intermediate, light and medium trucks twenty four.

The biggest percentage jump was abroad. International volumes rose one hundred and seventy seven percent, nearly triple, which the company ties to an order from Indonesia. At home, volumes rose thirty percent.

Did it win customers from rivals, or did the whole market grow? A bit of both, the company says. Industry volumes grew twenty eight percent, its own about thirty. Over the half year it held thirty six point two percent of registrations on the government's Vahan portal; in heavy trucks, fifty five point seven.

Not every line gained. Against last financial year, heavy trucks rose half a point, small commercial vehicles and pickups one point three, passenger carriers five. Yet intermediate, light and medium trucks fell from thirty eight to thirty six point three. The second quarter alone, thirty five point seven, was below the first quarter's thirty six point eight.

Now the puzzle from the start. Sales rose forty two percent. EBITDA, an operating profit measure the company defines itself, rose only thirty one. Out of every hundred rupees of sales, it kept eleven rupees seventy, against twelve rupees sixty a year earlier.

Why? The filings do not name one cause for the drop from a year earlier. The chief financial officer, G V Ramanan, says: 'Despite significant commodity cost pressures, particularly in steel and rubber, we maintained margins sequentially.' Against the June quarter, margins held.

The company's profit bridge shows the tug of war. Volume and mix added one thousand one hundred and fifty nine crore. Realisation, the slide's word for price, added one thousand and seventeen. Variable costs took away one thousand four hundred and sixteen.

The slide says the commodity impact was 'largely offset' by operating leverage, cost efficiencies and improved realisations. The press release says similar measures 'helped partially mitigate' it. The filings put no number on steel and rubber alone.

So did profit fall? No. On the company's own books, profit before exceptional items and tax rose fifty one percent, to two thousand six hundred and sixty crore. Lower finance costs and higher other income helped.

Then the cash. Free cash flow, on the company's own definition, was four thousand six hundred and six crore in the quarter, against two thousand two hundred and ten a year earlier. Where did it come from?

The table splits it. Cash profit after tax: two thousand two hundred and eighty seven crore. Changes in working capital, meaning stock and bills owed to and by the company, added two thousand six hundred and seventy nine. By our arithmetic, that is fifty eight percent of the quarter's free cash. A year earlier it was forty one percent.

The filing puts net cash at eleven thousand three hundred crore in the company itself. The group figure, fifteen thousand nine hundred crore, nets a subsidiary's debt against its Tata Capital shares at market value.

Now, Iveco. On the thirtieth of July, twenty twenty five, the filing says, the company and Iveco Group announced an agreement: an all-cash offer for Iveco's shares, to create a commercial vehicles group.

The offer leaves out Iveco's defence business. The filing gave about forty one thousand, three hundred and sixty three crore rupees as at the thirtieth of September, then, after the price change, a revised maximum of about forty two thousand, five hundred and sixty one crore.

Where does it stand? On the sixteenth of October, Iveco's shareholders approved all the offer's resolutions at an extraordinary meeting. The slide shows thirty five percent of shares tendered so far, as of the twenty second.

The acceptance period is due to close on the twenty sixth of October. Settlement is set for the thirtieth, the slide says, 'subject to Offer conditions being met'. The finance chief says the company is preparing 'for consolidation from next quarter'.

But. Here is what the filings do not say: how Tata Motors will pay. The company itself held eleven thousand three hundred crore of net cash; the group, fifteen thousand nine hundred. The maximum offer is about three point eight times the first and two point seven times the second, by our arithmetic. Net cash is only one possible source.
They do not say what share of Iveco the company needs for the offer to go through, or what the conditions are. Thirty five percent had tendered four days before the close.
And they do not say what Iveco will do to the margin or the debt once it is added in.

Closer in, the company's own warnings. Chief executive Girish Wagh says growth rates 'are expected to moderate in the second half against a higher base', and that commodity cost pressures 'remain a headwind'. In the same statement he says the company is 'well positioned for a robust FY27'.
Our reading: more than half of this quarter's free cash came from working capital, and working capital can swing back. The filings do not say whether it will.

The other side, from the same filings: net cash in the company rose from seven thousand five hundred crore in March to eleven thousand three hundred in September. And over the half year, free cash flow was five thousand seven hundred and twenty one crore.

So, back to fourteen euros forty. The company's own reason for the extra thirty cents: a slight delay. And the trucks: far more wholesaled, a little less kept of each rupee, with steel and rubber cited.
And the bill: settlement is set for the thirtieth of October, if the offer's conditions are met. If it is, the company says consolidation begins next quarter. That is the next filing to read.
